arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Glasgow argued Hungary and its railway are immune from suit. He stated the expropriation exception requires property to be exchanged for the stolen assets.
Mr. Dvoretzky argued Hungary lacks immunity for stealing property during the Holocaust. He stated the exception applies when a state possesses the expropriated property or property exchanged for it.
Mr. Joshi argued the commingling theory lacks support in the statute text. He noted words like that property and such property imply specific, identifiable assets.

paragraphs: This case tests the scope of the expropriation exception to sovereign immunity. The core dispute involves whether specific property requirements apply when funds are commingled.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Hungary wants the Court to dismiss the case. It argues the law requires specific, identifiable property for the exception to apply.
Simon wants the Court to allow the suit to continue. It argues the exception covers property exchanged for the stolen assets.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Hungary argues the statute text demands specific, identifiable property. It contends commingled funds do not meet this legal standard.
Simon argues the exception applies to property exchanged for the stolen assets. It contends the commercial nexus requirement is satisfied.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the reach of sovereign immunity for foreign states. It determines whether plaintiffs can access mixed financial accounts in U.S. courts. The outcome shapes future claims involving state-owned entities and historical property disputes.
